p: The oldest manuscripts have no subject. Later ones add "God" or "the Lord" (KJV).

readings.w: P23 (early 200s), Sinaiticus (01, 300s), Alexandrinus (02, 400s), Vaticanus (03, 300s), Ψ, 81, Sahidic and Bohairic Coptic; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: which he promised

readings.w: 33, 1739 and other minuscules, Old Latin, Vulgate, Peshitta Syriac
readings.en: which God promised

readings.w: C (04, 400s, with small differences), K, L, P, the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: which the Lord promised

why: The short reading is in the oldest witnesses, and copyists naturally supplied a subject, some "God" and some "the Lord". Two different additions point to an original without either. The meaning is the same: God is the one who promised.

a: no shifting, no shadow cast by turning
p: Sinaiticus as first written, Vaticanus and P23 have a genitive that changes the picture slightly.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (corrected), Alexandrinus, C, K, L, P, the Byzantine majority, Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: variation or shadow of turning
readings.plain: no shifting, no shadow cast by turning

readings.w: Sinaiticus as first written (01*), Vaticanus (03); P23 reads παραλλαγῆς with the same ending
readings.en: variation or (that) of the turning of a shadow
readings.plain: no shifting that belongs to the turning of the shadow

readings.w: 614, 1505 and related minuscules
readings.en: variation or turning of shadow
readings.plain: no shifting, no turning of shadow

why: The editions in this site's word list all print the reading of most manuscripts. The reading of Vaticanus and the first hand of Sinaiticus, with P23, is old; in this site's judgment its grammar is harder to construe. The sense hardly changes: God does not shift as the heavenly lights and their shadows do.

p: Most later manuscripts read "So then" (KJV "Wherefore"), which makes 1:19 a conclusion drawn from 1:18. The older ones read "You know" or "Know this".

readings.w: Sinaiticus as corrected (01², the first hand nearly the same), Vaticanus (03), C (04), 81, 945, 1739, Old Latin, Vulgate, Bohairic Coptic; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: ἴστε, ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοί· ἔστω δὲ
readings.en: you know (or: know this), my beloved brothers; but let

readings.w: P74 (as far as it can be read), Alexandrinus (02, with small differences), 2464, Sahidic Coptic
readings.orig: ἴστε δὲ, ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοί. ἔστω δὲ
readings.en: but know this, my beloved brothers. And let

readings.w: K, L, P (corrected), Ψ, 104, 614, 1505 and the Byzantine majority, Harklean Syriac; Textus Receptus (KJV "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let")
readings.en: so then, my beloved brothers, let

why: "You know" has the oldest manuscripts, and in capital letters ΙΣΤΕ and ΩΣΤΕ differ by one letter. "So then" is the smoother reading, since it joins the verse to what comes before and drops the "but" that follows. The Greek iste can be a statement ("you know") or a command ("know this"); this site's word list parses it as a command, and the Plain English Translation reads it as a statement that sums up 1:18.

a: Show me your faith apart from the works
p: The KJV's "shew me thy faith without thy works" follows one form of the Greek; the Byzantine text has "by your works".

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Alexandrinus (02, with a small change in word order after); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.orig: δεῖξόν μοι τὴν πίστιν σου χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων
readings.en: show me your faith without the works
readings.plain: Show me your faith apart from the works

readings.w: C (04, 400s); the Textus Receptus as printed by Scrivener (the KJV's Greek)
readings.orig: δεῖξόν μοι τὴν πίστιν σου χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων σου
readings.en: show me your faith without your works
readings.plain: Show me your faith apart from your works

readings.w: The Byzantine majority; Stephanus' 1550 Textus Receptus
readings.orig: δεῖξόν μοι τὴν πίστιν σου ἐκ τῶν ἔργων σου
readings.en: show me your faith by your works
readings.plain: Show me your faith by your works

why: The oldest manuscripts read "apart from the works", which makes the challenge sharp: faith without deeds cannot be shown at all. "By your works" makes the two halves of the verse say the same thing, which looks like a copyist's smoothing. The KJV, made from a Textus Receptus that here follows C, reads "without thy works".

t: "God is one" or "there is one God"?
p: The Greek manuscripts put the words in several orders. Some mean "God is one" (the Shema), others "there is one God".

readings.w: P74 (600s), Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vulgate, Coptic; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: God is one

readings.w: Vaticanus (03), 614, 1505 and others; Westcott and Hort
readings.en: there is one God

readings.w: The Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "there is one God")
readings.en: God is one

why: The editions print the reading of P74, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus. Vaticanus, as old as Sinaiticus, has the order "there is one God", and the Byzantine text has a third order. All three say the same thing, the faith of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4).

p: Many manuscripts read "dead" (KJV), as in 2:17 and 2:26. The oldest have "idle", a pun on "works".

readings.w: Vaticanus (03), C as first written (04*), 945, 1739 and others, Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic Coptic; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: idle, not working

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), C (corrected), K, L, P, Ψ, the Byzantine majority, Peshitta; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: dead
empty

why: "Dead" is easy to explain as a copyist repeating 2:17 and 2:26. "Idle" (arge, "without work") is a wordplay on "works" (erga) that is likely to be the writer's own.

p: The KJV's "how great a matter a little fire kindleth" follows manuscripts that read "a little" (oligon) for the first "how great" (helikon).

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: how great (or how small) a fire kindles how great a forest

readings.w: Alexandrinus (02, as far as it can be read), C (04), the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: a little fire kindles how great a forest

why: Using helikos twice, once for a small fire and once for a great forest, is the harder reading; "a little" looks like a copyist making the sense plain. The English comes out nearly the same either way. The Plain English Translation gives the first helikos the sense "how small" (see the note).

p: The older manuscripts have the unusual "the Lord and Father"; most later ones the familiar "God and Father" (KJV).

readings.w: P20 (200s), Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), C (04), P, Ψ, 33, 81, 1739, Old Latin, Peshitta; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: the Lord and Father

readings.w: K, L, the Byzantine majority, the Clementine Vulgate, Harklean Syriac; Textus Receptus (KJV "God, even the Father")
readings.en: God and Father

why: "God and Father" is a common New Testament phrase, and copyists would change the rare "Lord and Father" toward it, not the other way. The oldest witnesses agree on "Lord".

p: The KJV's "Ye adulterers and adulteresses" follows later manuscripts that add the masculine word.

readings.w: P100 (200s or 300s), Sinaiticus as first written (01*), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), 33, 81, 1739, Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: adulteresses

readings.w: Sinaiticus (corrector, 600s), K, L, P, Ψ, the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: adulterers and adulteresses

why: The shorter reading is far older. Copyists who took the word literally (as men's and women's adultery) would add "adulterers" so that the men were not left out. The feminine alone points to the prophets' picture of God's people as an unfaithful wife (see the note).

a: the spirit he placed to live in us
p: Two Greek verbs differ by one letter: "he caused to dwell" or "it dwelt" (KJV "the spirit that dwelleth in us").

readings.w: P74 (600s), Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Ψ, 1739 and others; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: which he caused to dwell in us
readings.plain: the spirit he placed to live in us

readings.w: K, L, P, the Byzantine majority, Old Latin, Vulgate, Syriac, Coptic; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: which dwelt in us
readings.plain: the spirit that lives in us

why: The two words sounded alike when read aloud, so either could come from the other. The causative "he made to dwell" has the oldest Greek support, and the printed editions follow it. With "dwelt", it is easier to take the spirit as the subject of "yearns", as the KJV does.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV have only "one lawgiver", without "and Judge".

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03) and most manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: lawgiver and judge

readings.w: The Byzantine text; Textus Receptus (KJV "There is one lawgiver")
readings.en: lawgiver

why: "And Judge" is in the oldest manuscripts and fits the verse, which is about judging (4:11-12). It may have dropped out because the two words end alike. A separate difference does not change the English: whether "Lawgiver" has the article. P74, P100, Vaticanus and P omit it, with SBLGNT and Westcott-Hort; Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, K, L, Ψ, 33, 81, 1739 and the Byzantine text have it, and NA28 prints it in square brackets.

a: You do not know what your life will be like tomorrow.
p: Many manuscripts add "for", which makes a separate question: "For what is your life?" (KJV).

readings.w: Sinaiticus as first written (01*), Vaticanus (03), 614, 1505 and others; SBLGNT, NA28
readings.orig: οὐκ ἐπίστασθε τὸ τῆς αὔριον ποία ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν
readings.en: you do not know what your life (will be) tomorrow
readings.plain: You do not know what your life will be like tomorrow.

readings.w: P74, P100, Sinaiticus (corrected), Alexandrinus (02), K, L, P, Ψ, the Byzantine majority, Old Latin, Vulgate; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: οὐκ ἐπίστασθε τὸ τῆς αὔριον. ποία γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ ὑμῶν;
readings.en: you do not know (what will be) tomorrow. For what is your life?
readings.plain: You do not know about tomorrow. For what is your life?

why: The witnesses are divided. SBLGNT, NA28 and THGNT leave out "for"; Tregelles and the Textus Receptus keep it. Without it, the words run on as one thought; with it, James asks a separate question. Either way, the next sentence answers: a puff of steam.

a: the pay you cheated them out of
p: SBL follows Sinaiticus and Vaticanus: wages "held back". NA28 and most manuscripts: wages "taken by fraud".

readings.w: Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (corrected), K, L, P, Ψ, 1739, the Byzantine majority, Vulgate; NA28, THGNT; Textus Receptus (KJV "kept back by fraud")
readings.en: which has been taken away by fraud by you
readings.plain: the pay you cheated them out of

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus as first written (03*); SBLGNT, Westcott and Hort
readings.en: which has been held back by you
readings.plain: the pay you held back from them

why: This is a place where the SBL edition and NA28 differ. NA28, which takes its text of James from the Editio Critica Maior, prints "defrauded" (as the edition marks of this site's word list show), the reading of most witnesses, early and late. "Held back" is the rarer word and may be original. The Plain English Translation follows NA28 here. Either way the wages were never paid, against Deuteronomy 24:15.

a: the early and the late rains
p: The oldest text says only "the early and the late". Later manuscripts spell out "rain"; Sinaiticus has "fruit".

readings.w: P74 (600s), Vaticanus (03), 1739 and others, Old Latin, Vulgate, Sahidic Coptic; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: until it receives early and late
readings.plain: the early and the late rains

readings.w: Alexandrinus (02), K, L, P, Ψ, the Byzantine majority, Syriac; Textus Receptus (KJV "the early and latter rain")
readings.orig: ἕως λάβῃ ὑετὸν πρώϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον
readings.en: until it receives the early and late rain
readings.plain: the early and the late rains

readings.w: Sinaiticus as corrected (01²; the apparatus puts the first hand with it in parentheses), 255, 398, 1175, Old Latin ms ff, the Harklean Syriac margin, Bohairic Coptic in part
readings.orig: ἕως λάβῃ καρπὸν πρόϊμον καὶ ὄψιμον
readings.en: until it receives early and late fruit
readings.plain: the early and the late fruit

why: Every Jewish reader knew "the early rain and the late rain" (Deuteronomy 11:14), so the oldest text needed no noun; English does, and the Plain English Translation supplies "rains". Later copyists supplied it too. The reading "fruit" has the farmer wait for an early and a late crop instead of the rains.

a: you saw the outcome the Lord gave
p: The Byzantine text reads the command "see" for "you saw". The two Greek words differ by one letter.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03) and others; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Textus Receptus (KJV "have seen")
readings.en: you saw the outcome of the Lord
readings.plain: you saw the outcome the Lord gave

readings.w: Alexandrinus (02), the Byzantine text
readings.en: see the outcome of the Lord
readings.plain: see the outcome the Lord gave

why: Eidete ("you saw") and idete ("see!") sounded alike. "You saw" pairs with "you have heard" just before it: the readers heard of Job's endurance and saw how the Lord ended his story.

p: The Byzantine text has no subject: "for he is very tender-hearted".

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03, with a small difference); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Textus Receptus (KJV "that the Lord is very pitiful")
readings.en: the Lord is very compassionate

readings.w: The Byzantine text
readings.en: he is very compassionate

why: The oldest manuscripts name "the Lord". Without it the subject is still the Lord of the clause before, so the meaning does not change.

a: so that you do not come under judgment
p: The Byzantine text reads "so that you do not fall into hypocrisy", a different division of the same letters.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; the Textus Receptus as printed by Scrivener (KJV "lest ye fall into condemnation")
readings.en: so that you do not fall under judgment
readings.plain: so that you do not come under judgment

readings.w: The Byzantine majority; Stephanus' 1550 Textus Receptus
readings.en: so that you do not fall into hypocrisy
readings.plain: so that you do not fall into hypocrisy

why: In letters written without spaces, hypo krisin ("under judgment") and hypokrisin ("hypocrisy") are almost the same. The oldest manuscripts read "under judgment", which matches "or you will be judged" in 5:9.

p: Vaticanus and a few other witnesses have no "him". NA28 prints the word in square brackets.

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Ψ (with a small difference), 048 (as far as it can be read), the Byzantine majority; SBLGNT, THGNT, NA28 (in brackets), Textus Receptus (KJV "anointing him with oil")
readings.en: having anointed him with oil

readings.w: Vaticanus (03), P, 1243 and a few others, Old Latin ms ff, some Vulgate manuscripts, Sahidic Coptic in part; Westcott-Hort
readings.en: having anointed with oil

why: The pronoun changes nothing: either way the sick person is the one anointed. Square brackets in NA28 mark a word whose place in the text the editors held to be uncertain.

p: The KJV's "Confess your faults one to another" follows the Byzantine text, which reads "trespasses" and has no "so then".

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: so confess your sins to one another

readings.w: The Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV "faults")
readings.en: confess your trespasses to one another

why: The oldest manuscripts have "so then" (oun), which ties the confession to the healing of 5:14-15, and the ordinary word "sins".

a: will save his soul from death
p: The Byzantine text lacks "his": the KJV reads "shall save a soul from death".

readings.w: Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), P, 33, 1739 and others, Vulgate, Syriac; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.en: will save his soul from death
readings.plain: will save his soul from death

readings.w: P74 (600s), Vaticanus (03), 614 and others
readings.en: will save a soul from his death
readings.plain: will save a soul from his death

readings.w: K, L, Ψ, the Byzantine majority; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: will save a soul from death
readings.plain: will save a soul from death

why: The witnesses disagree on where "his" stands, or whether it is there at all, which may show that copyists felt the ambiguity of whose soul is meant (see the note). The Plain English Translation follows SBLGNT and NA28.
